newsitem.title: USA: Kasparov issues new challenge to Deep Blue.
newsitem.headline: Kasparov issues new challenge to Deep Blue.

text.p: World chess champion Garry Kasparov said on Friday he had recovered from his stunning defeat only days ago by the IBM supercomputer Deep Blue and wanted to play the machine again before the end of the year in a winner-takes-all match.

Kasparov told Reuters in an interview he was prepared to play the match in September or October in New York but under different conditions from the six-game contest that ended painfully and bitterly for him on Sunday and gloriously for a team of computer scientists.
"I'm ready to play all or nothing," Kasparov said. "It's very important, I'm not here to grab money even if I lose." Kasparov won $400,000 for last week's match.

"I want to play a longer match of 10 games with better conditions for a human player," the 34-year-old Russian grandmaster said. He said he wanted more rest between each game. "I've learned a lot and will also demand 10 games of Deep Blue played against a grandmaster or any other computer in the presence of my representative."
Before, during and after the $1.1 million match, Kasparov complained that the conditions were essentially unfair because he had no access to the computer program's practice games in the laboratory.
In Friday's interview, he acknowledged that he had agreed to those conditions but said he also felt unexpected hostility toward him from Deep Blue team members during the match.
A spokeswoman for the company said it was difficult to respond to Kasparov's comments. "We realise that he was upset and while it was uncomfortable we're looking beyond that now."

Kasparov defeated a weaker and less sophisticated version of Deep Blue in Philadelphia in February 1996 in similar match conditions -- six games that can each last several hou IBM said it was gathering a group of people together to examine whether another match could be held with Kasparov, considered by most experts to be the best player in the history of the ancient game.
"I think we are considering that right now and we also have gotten several requests from other grandmasters for a match," Deep Blue team manager Chung-Jen "CJ" Tan said.
Tan said those included Kasparov's arch-rival Anatoly Karpov, champion of the International Chess Federation (FIDE), which Kasparov left in 1993 to form the rival Professional Chess Association.

Women's world champion Susan Polgar has also issued a challenge to play Deep Blue, an IBM RS/6000 SP parallel processor with specialised microchips for chess that can examine hundreds of millions of moves per second.

Kasparov, who suffered an astonishing failure of nerve in the final game that cost him the match and the winner's prize of $700,000, also said he wanted an independent specialist watching Deep Blue's computer screen during the next contest and an independent organiser.

IBM sponsored the $1.1 million match, organised it with assistance from the Association of Computing and Machinery and enjoyed a bonanza of publicity. The competition drew 500 people to each game at a Manhattan exhibition centre and was followed by millions on the World Wide Web.

Kasparov said he did not expect last week's match to become so competitive because it had also been billed as an experiment in IBM's research of computers that can make complex simultaneous calculations at high speeds.
"I'm not complaining about this any longer because it's history. I want to play a real competitive match where science and challenge are separated," he said.
The match contained some tense moments and acrimony, particularly the champion's insinuation after his defeat in the second game that IBM might be cheating by human intervention.
"I think game two posed too many questions and I think it is in the interest of the IBM team to answer those questions," Kasparov said on Friday.

The game, won by the system, was hailed by expert observers as the best ever played by a computer, even though analysis showed that the human player had in fact resigned in a drawn position, something Kasparov never recovered from psychologically.

"They should not say 'it's not your business' because no computer in the world will reconstruct the steps ... they will not give you the same result," Kasparov said, referring to a key position in the game when the system effectively "changed its mind" as it was calculating its options.

Kasparov said he admired the computer scientists' work on the chess-playing machine but said, "I think they will have to deal with the world of science, they have to give these explanations. I believe that at one point even the inventors of Deep Blue don't know the implications of Deep Blue's decisions."
